articles.title: US seeks a cheaper alternative to MQ-9 as India seeks these drones for USD 3 billion
articles.summary: International News: The US Air Force wants a cheaper and faster replacement for its dwindling fleet of MQ-9A Reapers. The force is seeking a unit price of around USD 10 m.
articles.body: The US Air Force wants a cheaper and faster replacement for its dwindling fleet of MQ-9A Reapers. The force is seeking a unit price of around USD 10 million for the Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), which is considerably less than the USD 30-50 million dollars for a fully equipped aircraft. The urgency to bring in the new aircraft is caused by the loss of many of these aircraft in the ongoing operations in Iran as well as over Yemen.The new drone programme, called the Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), is expected to retain the MQ-9A's ISR and strike capability according to Air Force Lieutenant General Christopher Niemi, the service's Chief Modernization Officer. Programme requirements call for a speed of at least 200 knots, a payload capacity of 2,800 pounds, an unrefuelled combat radius of 2,300 nautical miles (4,200 km), a ferry range of up to 8,000 nautical miles (14,000 km) and the ability to operate from runways as short as 6,000 feet. The MMA is expected to be built around a modular, open-architecture design that makes future upgrades easier.General Atomics, the original maker of the Reaper, has already responded with its Wildfire drone, pitched as delivering everything that made the Reaper effective, only sooner and at a fraction of the cost. With combat losses mounting and the Pentagon keen to field something more expendable and affordable at scale, the MMA programme looks set to reshape how America's next generation of drones gets built.The US military has lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during its ongoing conflict with Iran, close to a quarter of the roughly 185-strong fleet it started with, split between 165 with the Air Force and 20 with the Marine Corps. Operating heavily around the Strait of Hormuz, the drones have proven easy targets for Iran and its regional proxies given their slow speed and low-altitude profile, with some losses also traced to communication link failures rather than enemy fire.For nearly two decades, the Reaper has been the quiet workhorse of America's Central Command operations, flying surveillance and strike missions across Iraq, Afghanistan, Yemen and Syria in largely uncontested skies. That flight profile, slow and predictable, worked brilliantly against terror organisations without an effective air defence capability. Against Iran, the same characteristics have turned into a liability, making it a comparatively easy kill.India, too, is buying into this same platform across all three services, eight each for the Army and Air Force and 15 for the Navy, in a deal worth over USD 3 billion, drawn largely by its 40-hour endurance and the surveillance picture that offers over the Indian Ocean and along India's land borders. Induction is expected by 2029, with 21 of the drones to be assembled domestically and 34 per cent local component sourcing. The Navy, which already leases two Reapers, has just signed a fresh Rs 1,943 crore deal to extend that lease by 30 months, underlining just how central this aircraft has become to India's own surveillance plans, contested skies notwithstanding.

articles.title: One in five German firms feels impact of foreign hybrid threats
articles.summary: One in five companies in Germany says it is feeling the effects of hybrid threats from abroad, including cyberattacks, disinformation, espionage and sabotage...
articles.body:
One in five companies in Germany is feeling the effects of foreign hybrid threats, including cyberattacks, disinformation, espionage, and sabotage, according to a survey by the German Economic Institute (IW).

Larger firms with more than 250 employees are particularly affected by these hybrid threats, prompting companies to improve security at their sites or disrupting day-to-day operations.

Information and communications companies perceived the greatest risks from hybrid attacks, followed by firms involved in energy and water supplies and waste management, highlighting the need for better preparedness in defending against such threats in Germany.

One in five companies in Germany says it is feeling the effects of hybrid threats from abroad, including cyberattacks, disinformation, espionage and sabotage, according to a survey by the German Economic Institute (IW).

The institute surveyed 1,041 companies and found that larger firms with more than 250 employees were particularly affected.

Companies said the threats had prompted them to improve security at their sites or had disrupted their day-to-day operations.

By sector, information and communications companies perceived the greatest risks, followed by firms involved in energy and water supplies and waste management.

Hybrid attacks can involve a combination of military, economic, intelligence and propaganda measures. They also include cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns aimed, for example, at influencing public opinion ahead of elections.

Siemens Energy chief executive Christian Bruch earlier this week told dpa that the threat level had risen significantly over the past 12 to 18 months.

He called for a civilian emergency plan to help respond to crises and protect electricity and water infrastructure as well as food supplies.

The IW said its findings showed that Germany needed to become better prepared to defend itself against such threats.

While many companies had increased investment in IT security and digital infrastructure, only a small proportion had better secured their energy supplies or drawn up emergency plans for failures of critical infrastructure.

"The lack of preparedness has a destabilizing effect on the functioning of the economy and society," the IW warned.

articles.title: In 1974, President Ronald Reagan bought the 688-acre Rancho del Cielo near Santa Barbara; sold 24 years later, it became a California State Landmark in 2002
articles.summary: US News: Ronald and Nancy Reagan bought Rancho del Cielo, which is a 688-acre ranch in the Santa Ynez Mountains near Santa Barbara, in 1974, near the end of Re.
articles.body: Ronald and Nancy Reagan bought Rancho del Cielo, which is a 688-acre ranch in the Santa Ynez Mountains near Santa Barbara, in 1974, near the end of Reagan's second term as California governor. The property became their private retreat and later served as Reagan's Western White House during his presidency.The Ronald Reagan Presidential Library describes the ranch as a working property with a small house, animals, horses and a lake. Reagan used it regularly during his years in the White House, often returning to the ranch between presidential duties.A working ranch, not a presidential estateThe Reagan Library describes the ranch as an informal ranch without central heating, maintained by a small staff. Cattle, horses and dogs lived on the property, while Reagan spent time riding and working outdoors. The ranch also had a small lake where he and Nancy Reagan went canoeing.The property became part of Reagan's life well before he entered the White House, and after his 1980 election, the ranch took on an additional role as a place where the president could work and receive visitors away from Washington. The Reagan Library's records of presidential trips show repeated visits to Rancho del Cielo throughout the 1980s. Reagan also used the ranch for radio addresses and meetings.The Western White HouseDuring Reagan's presidency, Rancho del Cielo became known as the Western White House. The ranch hosted foreign leaders and other prominent visitors, including Queen Elizabeth II, Prince Philip, British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.The Reagan Library says the ranch was used frequently during the administration as a vacation home, and its location in the mountains northwest of Santa Barbara provided a setting where Reagan could combine recreation with work. Reagan's activities there were often less formal than those at the White House. He rode horses, worked on fences and spent time around the ranch's animals. The property also became associated with some of his most recognizable outdoor photographs. The ranch remained in the family's ownership after Reagan left the presidency in 1989, and Reagan's final visit to the property came before his health made continued trips difficult.The ranch was sold in 1998The Reagans eventually put Rancho del Cielo on the market, and in 1998, Young America's Foundation purchased the 688-acre property with the intention of preserving it. Young America's Foundation says it acquired Rancho del Cielo on April 21, 1998, with the Reagan family's support. The organization has continued to preserve the ranch and use it for educational programs.The sale came 24 years after the Reagans had bought the ranch. It remained associated with Reagan's presidency and his personal life rather than being redeveloped as a private property. Young America's Foundation describes the ranch as Reagan's home for nearly 25 years and says it has preserved the property since the 1998 acquisition.A state landmarkRancho del Cielo received another designation in 2002, when the property was dedicated as a California State Landmark by the Native Sons of the Golden West. The designation came four years after Young America's Foundation acquired the ranch. The organization has continued to maintain the property in its historical form and use it for programs and special events.The ranch is not operated like a conventional public museum, as access is primarily connected to Young America's Foundation programs and special events, while the organization's Reagan Ranch Center in downtown Santa Barbara provides a more accessible public exhibit about Reagan and the property. Today, the 688-acre ranch remains in the hands of Young America's Foundation. The original ranch house, lake, barns and other features remain part of the property associated with Reagan's years there.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: As Europe emerges as a higher education hub for Indians, local language skills take centre stage
articles.summary: Europe News: Choosing Continental Europe for higher education is no longer just an emerging trend—it represents a fundamental shift in the Indian study abroad mark.
articles.body: Choosing Continental Europe for higher education is no longer just an emerging trend—it represents a fundamental shift in the Indian study abroad market. Driven by tightening visa regulations and immigration pushback in traditional destinations like the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, Indian families are looking beyond the ‘Big Four’.But instead of treating the region as a monolith, Indian students are carefully evaluating European destinations city by city. While tuition costs, housing, language barriers, and post-study work rights heavily influence these decisions, academic strength remains the ultimate priority. Furthermore, as AI reshapes education and employment, innovative opportunities are drawing students away from traditional corridors. While Germany leads the charge as a primary European hub, France and Italy are experiencing rapid growth, with Spain, Portugal, Austria, the Netherlands, and Malta gaining significant momentum. Germany attracts a large number of Indian students for engineering and STEM subjects, while the strongest interest from Indian students going to France has been concentrated in business and management. Sectors such as gastronomy, hospitality, fashion, luxury and design also attract Indian students to France. Italy offers a combination of comparatively affordable education, scholarships and specialised programmes in engineering, design, architecture and business.Data science, AI, climate and sustainability and environment-related courses have become a big draw for Indian students at European universities. The widespread availability of English-taught programmes and increasingly formalized post-graduation employment pathways have strengthened the region's long-term attraction.Germany is the clearest example of a significant growth in enrolment of Indian students, with India now the largest source country. In 2025, there were 69,816 Indian students studying for degree courses, including bachelor's, master's, and PhD in Germany - a rise of over 10,000 from the previous year, according to DAAD, the German Academic Exchange Service.“International students are allowed to work part-time 140 full days or 280 half days in a variety of capacities such as assistants and support in shops, businesses, hospitality industry, libraries and teaching assistants. International students are allowed to stay in Germany for 18 months after completion of their degree. During this time, they can look for an appropriate job or prepare for the next degree they would like to pursue,” says Aditi Gosavi, senior advisor with the New Delhi regional office of DAAD. The German job market is welcoming towards international students and many Indian students have made Germany their home. This welcoming policy landscape has made Germany an attractive long-term destination for global talent. Gosavi adds: “Indian employees have emerged as the highest earners among foreign workers in Germany largely in technical and academic roles.”Germany offers a distinct cost advantage for Indian students through its state-funded public universities, which charge minimal to no tuition fees beyond a semester contribution of roughly €300 that often covers local transport and campus services. Beyond tuition, students typically require around €1,000 per month for living expenses—including housing, food, study materials, health insurance, and leisure—though actual costs vary depending on the city and individual lifestyle. In France, costs depend heavily on location, with living expenses in Paris predictably higher than in regional cities. Annual tuition at public universities and engineering schools costs approximately ₹3.4 lakh for bachelor’s programmes and ₹4.4 lakh for master’s degrees, while university cafeterias offer universally accessible, subsidized €1 meals to help offset daily expenses.However, Europe’s growing appeal extends far beyond affordability, feels Adarsh Khandelwal, cofounder and director of education consultancy Collegify. According to him, as Indian students become more sophisticated consumers of international education, they are actively targeting specific academic ecosystems: Germany for engineering, technology, and advanced manufacturing; France for luxury, hospitality, management, and finance; and the Netherlands for sustainability and innovation. “While rising costs and tightening immigration policies in traditional destinations have encouraged families to diversify, Europe’s primary driver is value and opportunity. Germany pairs tuition-free, world-class education with a deep industrial sector and favourable post-study work pathways. Meanwhile, France is capitalizing on the high quality of its prestigious Grandes Écoles with strong government backing, and aiming to welcome 30,000 Indian students by 2030.”While Europe’s rising appeal stems fundamentally from affordability, experts view this factor less as a discount price point and more as an intentional policy choice that treats higher education as public infrastructure.“Continental Europe has seen the most pronounced shift over the last several intakes, and our data bears that out,” notes Akshay Chaturvedi, founder & CEO of study abroad consultancy firm Leverage Edu. “It is the fastest-accelerating region on our platform, with Germany nearly doubling year-on-year, Italy and France growing fivefold or more, and strong momentum building across Ireland, Malta, and Spain.”Chaturvedi highlights that this student movement, especially towards Germany, is heavily concentrated in engineering and applied sciences, indicating that applicants are driven as much by Europe’s industrial depth as by lower costs.Language remains an important consideration when navigating education and careers in Europe. While there are many excellent English-taught programmes across continental Europe, students cannot assume that because their degree is in English, their career can also be built entirely in English. Local language proficiency and adapting to local professional culture often determine employment options.“Choosing France for an English-taught program should drive the need for French language classes, and in the immersive context the students are in, a good command of French should take no more than a year. Landing an internship in France without being able to communicate in French is almost impossible,” says Consul General of France in Kolkata Thierry Morel.And as more and more Indians, especially those from STEM backgrounds, are now considering Germany as a top destination for working and studying; language is an important aspect and speaking the German language improves job and future prospects.“Within the pathways for Indian students in Europe, the variable that matters most is language. Students admitted and taught in English will still find that local proficiency shapes how quickly they move into the workforce, and those who begin that preparation alongside their application rather than after graduation have consistently had the strongest outcomes,” says Leverage Edu’s Chaturvedi.The number of Indian students choosing France for their higher education is growing every year and reached 12,000 last year, with an approximate increase of 15 to 20 per cent every year. However, France is not particularly expecting to scavenge the students who did not make it to other countries such as the US, Canada, the UK and Australia because of the recent pushback, and students should come to France as their first and informed choice, explains Consul General Morel.“This growth can be explained by a few factors including increased awareness about France and the quality of its education; growing number of English taught programmes in France; recognition of degrees between France and India and opportunities for our alumni, that include a post-study resident permit of up to two years for master’s graduates allowing them to look for a job or set up a business,” he says.Even as Indian students weigh tuition costs and post-study work visas across Europe, the search for housing has shifted from a post-visa afterthought to a primary decision-making factor.“Accommodation is one of the biggest practical challenges for Indian students, especially in Europe’s popular university cities. Demand spikes around academic intakes while university housing remains limited, forcing international students to compete with local residents and young professionals for private rentals,” says Saurabh Arora, Founder & CEO of University Living, a tech-enabled platform for student housing.Arora notes that this pressure is sharpest in major student hubs, where rents are high and affordable options sell out quickly. While conditions vary by city, the underlying shortage is widespread.“Navigating local rental contracts, security deposits, guarantor rules, and language barriers from abroad adds another layer of difficulty for Indian students—along with the risk of scams and hidden fees,” Arora explains. He urges students to start their search immediately upon receiving an offer letter. “First, look into university residences, then compare verified private housing and shared flats. Always check what the rent covers, clarify cancellation policies, and never transfer money through unverified channels.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1831, Sweden planted 300,000 oak trees for future warships; 144 years later, the Navy didn't need them anymore
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the early 19th century, Sweden began an extraordinary project on the island of ‘Visingsö.’ Hundreds of thousands of oak trees were planted to secur.
articles.body: In the early 19th century, Sweden began an extraordinary project on the island of ‘Visingsö.’ Hundreds of thousands of oak trees were planted to secure timber for naval ships that would be built far in the future. Oak was strong, durable and widely valued for wooden shipbuilding, but the trees required generations to reach a useful size. The people behind the project were therefore planning far beyond their own lifetimes. Yet technology changed before the forest could fulfil its purpose. By the time the oaks had matured, naval shipbuilding had moved away from wooden hulls and towards new materials. The forest had spent more than a century growing for a Navy that no longer needed it. Its story, however, did not end there. The trees remained standing, eventually finding different uses and becoming a lasting reminder of an ambitious plan overtaken by progress.Why did Sweden plant 300,000 oak trees for future warshipsAccording to Atlas Obscura, the project began around 1830, following the Napoleonic Wars. The Swedish Crown wanted to secure a future supply of oak for its naval ships and began searching for a suitable place to grow the trees. That search led to ‘Visingsö,’ an island in Lake Vättern. Representatives sent to examine the island reportedly noticed several impressive oak trees growing near a small farmhouse. The conditions appeared suitable, and the Royal Navy decided to establish a large oak plantation there.Over the following decade, about 300,000 oaks were planted. The project was based on an exceptionally long view of the future. Oak trees grow slowly, meaning the people who began the work knew they would probably never see the forest reach its intended purpose. The trees were grown to produce straight, useful timber The plantation was carefully designed rather than left to develop naturally. Atlas Obscura reports that other species, including ash, elm, maple, beech and silver fir, were planted among the oaks. These surrounding trees encouraged the oaks to grow upwards as they competed for light. This produced tall, straight trunks, making the timber better suited to the needs of shipbuilding. The forest eventually covered nearly 900 acres, or around 360 hectares. Its trees represented a vast supply of timber that Sweden expected to use when they had grown large enough.What happened when Visingsö’s oak trees were finally ready for the NavyThe forest reached maturity at the wrong moment for the plan that had created it. By around 1975, 144 years after the first trees were planted, the Swedish Navy no longer needed vast quantities of oak for warships. Naval technology had changed during the decades the trees were growing, and wooden vessels had been replaced by ships made from iron and steel. According to Atlas Obscura, the trees had become suitable for the purpose for which they were planted, but that purpose had disappeared. The Swedish Navy had successfully waited for the forest to grow, only to find that shipbuilding had moved in a completely different direction.How did the naval oak forest find a new purposeThe Visingsö oaks did not become worthless when the Navy stopped needing them. Their high-quality timber could still be used in other ways. As per Atlas Obscura, the wood from the forest is suitable for flooring, veneers and furniture. The oak is also used to make high-quality ‘whisky barrels.’ Today, the forest has become part of Visingsö's identity and a reminder of one of Sweden's unique long-term projects. Visitors can reach the island by boat from Gränna and explore a landscape created for a military future that never arrived.A long-term plan overtaken by technological changeThe Visingsö oak forest shows the difficulty of planning for a distant future. The Swedish Crown made a serious attempt to prepare for needs that lay generations ahead, but it could not predict how rapidly naval technology would change. Nearly two centuries later, the forest remains a striking legacy of that decision. The people who planted the trees prepared for a future fleet of wooden warships. Instead, the oaks grew into a different future altogether. The forest's original purpose may have vanished, but the trees survived. Their story now stands as a reminder that nature works on a timescale that technology does not always follow.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Very strange’: Minor's counsel questions police intent after Swatantra Bhardwaj’s one-day custody
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Counsel for the CJP protester on Saturday questioned the manner in which social media 'influencer' Swatantra Bhardwaj was produced before a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Counsel for the CJP protester on Saturday questioned the manner in which social media 'influencer' Swatantra Bhardwaj was produced before a judge and remanded to one-day police custody in connection with the alleged assault on the protester’s father during a July 20 protest at Jantar Mantar.“It is very strange. We were all present in the court and waiting for the hearing to begin. Later, we came to know that legal aid counsel joined through video conferencing and the accused was presented before the judge at his residence,” Rishav Ranjan, counsel for the CJP protester, said.Ranjan also questioned why police sought only one day’s custody in what he described as a serious offence and said the legal team had not been given details of the provisions added to the FIR.“One-day police custody was sought in such a serious offence. We did not receive any details as to what charges were added and what additions were made to the FIR. I don't know what is being hidden. Delhi Police have not made any official statement regarding the sections, so far,” he said.Bhardwaj arrested, sent to one-day custodyBhardwaj was arrested by Delhi Police on Saturday, a day after he was detained in Uttar Pradesh’s Bulandshahr in connection with the alleged assault during the CJP protest at Jantar Mantar.He was produced before the concerned judge at the judge’s residence at the Karkardooma court complex and remanded to one-day police custody, news agency ANI reported.The development came after the CJP protested outside Parliament Street police station on Friday, demanding action against Bhardwaj. Police subsequently added provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and criminal intimidation to the FIR relating to the alleged assault.A fresh FIR was also registered against Bhardwaj under the POCSO Act following a complaint by the minor CJP protester alleging online threats and harassment. The case invokes provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Information Technology Act.Case followed Bhardwaj's Jantar Mantar claimsThe case had escalated after Bhardwaj made remarks in a podcast about the Jantar Mantar confrontation, claiming that he had “cracked the skull” of the protester’s father.He later said he had acted in self-defence and claimed he was surrounded by a group of people during the incident.Delhi Police had earlier said the injuries suffered by the protester’s father were “simple” in nature and were caused by a steel bracelet.Bhardwaj was detained in Bulandshahr on Friday after CJP representatives demanded his arrest. articles.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows true size of all countries
articles.summary: Africa-led campaign asks governments, schools and tech firms to move away from the centuries-old Mercator projection
articles.body:
The UN general assembly has voted to replace the traditional Mercator map with the Equal Earth projection to provide a more accurate representation of the size of all nations.

The resolution, sponsored by Togo and supported by 164 nations including the UK, aims to establish proportionally accurate maps as a new global norm without banning the Mercator projection outright.

The campaign, endorsed by the African Union, seeks to address the issue of "cartographic colonialism" and promote a more equitable representation of the world's continents, particularly Africa.

The UN general assembly has voted to replace the traditional world map with one that more accurately reflects the size of all nations.

The approved resolution calls for the world to move away from the traditional Mercator map , which shrinks the size of Africa and exaggerates northern landmasses.

The "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by Togo, passed with the support of 164 nations, including the UK. The US was the only nation to vote against it, with six other abstentions.

The resolution is non-binding, but asks governments, schools, international organisations, and technology companies to adopt the Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps wherever the true scale of continents matters, with the aim of establishing more proportionally accurate maps as a new global norm. It does not seek to ban the Mercator projection outright.

The Mercator projection, which is currently used worldwide, increases distortion the further a region sits from the equator. Since Africa straddles the equator, it seems comparatively smaller than its actual size, while Europe, North America, Greenland , and Russia all appear substantially larger than they are.

As a result, Africa, along with Latin America, India and other equatorial regions, appear much smaller relative to northern countries than their true area. The map, for example, depicts Africa as similar in size to Greenland, despite the continent being 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

In a briefing to the African Group at the UN this week, Togo's foreign minister Robert Dussey said the importance of the issue went beyond geography.

"A map is never neutral," Mr Dussey reasoned. "It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood, and may, sometimes from the earliest years of schooling, perpetuate representations that do not correspond to geographic reality."

"Africa is not asking for preferential treatment," he said. "Africa is asking that its reality, aspirations and contribution to the international system be duly taken into account."

"I'm an academic before a politician," Mr Dussey said. "As an academic, I say we have to have as large a consensus as possible, because we are here at the UN, we never know."

A petition on the fundraising platform Change for the campaign, called #CorrectTheMap, had gathered around 11,000 signatures ahead of the vote. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and asked Togo to lead the push for its adoption at the UN.

"As Africa becomes increasingly central to solving global challenges," the petition says, "it is critical to represent its true scale."

Historians and geographers have long argued that the Mercator map reflects Western assumptions about the world, and some campaigners have used the term "cartographic colonialism" to denounce what they have described as its negative effects.

German historian Arno Peters was one of the most prominent critics of the projection, launching an alternative map based on the Gall-Peters projection in 1973. Togo's campaign is instead promoting the 2018 Equal Earth map, developed by an international team of cartographers, which supporters say offers a more accurate representation of the size of every continent.

Mr Dussey connected the map campaign to another African Union-backed resolution passed at the UN in March which described the transatlantic slave trade as the "gravest crime against humanity" and was approved by 123 states, with three against and 52 abstentions.

Togo's government is now set to hold an event in the capital, Lomé, with Unesco, the African Union, and technology companies including Google Maps in the first quarter of next year to work out how the change may be implemented.

English elegance During its 228 years of existence, the London restaurant Rules – established by Thomas Rule in 1798 – has welcomed everyone from literary giant Charles Dickens to pop queen Madonna. Vibrant red flags and gold-trimmed awnings announce this historic eatery in Covent Garden and, once inside, you’re instantly transported to another era. Every inch of wall space is covered with vintage mirrors, statues and busts, alongside countless drawings, cartoons and paintings. The gold-stencilled lettering on the window — “Oysters. Pies. Pudding.” — outlines the traditional British fare on offer. From rabbit to guinea fowl, it sells more game than any other restaurant in the UK, and as for desserts, it’s strictly old school. Feast your eyes here. An undersea cable for an electricity project was set to go right through the popular mound of stones, but protesters were not having it. Airing in the US later this month, “The Traitors: New Blood” is the first all-civilian version of the show hosted by Alan Cumming and, as with the other seasons, is filmed in the Scottish Highlands. CNN subscribers can watch Cumming explore the Highlands in the opening episode of our 2025 travel series “My Happy Place”: Stream now. That could be all set to change, however, as last year UNESCO named Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh state in northern India, a Creative City of Gastronomy. Get there while it’s hot. A little further east, in Indonesia, there’s a fine-dining revolution going on. That means reimagining its famous spices into sophisticated high-level experiences, while sharing the stories of Indonesian flavor through a different lens. articles.title: Richard Hammond to find a way to share Welsh mansion with bats
articles.summary: Rare bats found at the Georgian mansion have delayed his plans to build a padel court and luxury car garage.
articles.body:
Former Top Gear star Richard Hammond has said he will "find a way" of sharing his new £2m home with rare bats that have paused his renovation plans.

Work to add a padel court and luxury car garage hit the brakes after a survey found several species of bat, including the common pipistrelle and soprano pipistrelles, foraging in the grounds.

The 56-year-old bought the 19th Century Georgian mansion in Llanwenarth, near Abergavenny, in November 2025.

"If I have to share it with the bats, I'll find a way of sharing it with the bats," Hammond told BBC Wales.

"You don't move somewhere as beautiful as this and expect to stamp out everything that already lives there... I'm sure there's room for the bats and me in Abergavenny."

The survey ahead of the planned renovation work at the property identified a legal requirement to apply for a protected species development licence in order for it to continue.

Explaining the move to Monmouthshire, Hammond said: "It's no secret that I got divorced last year, sadly, and I knew I had to move.

"I saw the house advertised and thought, 'there must be something wrong with that' but went to have a look at it.

"I fell head over heels in love with the house."

Hammond and ex-wife Mindy divorced following 23 years of marriage. They have two daughters.

He said he had viewed the property, set within 21 acres, another five times before buying it.

"Every single week I've discovered another reason to be delighted that I live there," he said.

"I've never been happier moving in anywhere."

Hammond said he plans to look after the home, as the previous owners had, but hopes to renovate some aspects.

"I'm very lucky in that most of what I'm having to do is just make it fit for my lifestyle rather than repair it. So it could be a long project. It's not going to be finished in a month or two.

"I'll do nothing to change the look of the place. Why would I? You don't buy something beautiful and then deface it," he said.

Planning documents lodged for the property said it "occupies an elevated position overlooking the Usk Valley, set within extensive landscaped grounds and the remnant parkland of a former estate".

The estate included "historic outbuildings, former stables, ancillary structures and formal gardens", and sat within Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, also known as the Brecon Beacons .

The documents stated the applications were for "alterations and repairs, new extensions, reversal of modern alterations, replacement windows and forming new doorways".

A "critical element of the proposals" would be a garage that would store Hammond's "collection of historic and specialist vehicles", the application said.

A new padel court and "associated pavilion" would also replace an existing tennis court.

The bat survey commissioned ahead of the proposed building work found "bat activity levels in the immediate vicinity of the building complex were moderate, and the surrounding habitats supported foraging and dispersal by a diverse assemblage of bat species".

Other types of bats found included brown long-eared, noctule and Leisler's. Serotine were also occasionally seen within the same area.

A protected species development licence would be required from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), in order to carry out the proposed barn conversion.

The report said this must be done alongside "appropriate measures" to prevent harm of the bat species concerned.

Without doing so, Hammond would be unable to carry out his plans to renovate the barn.

"The habitats on site at The Pentre support a diverse assemblage of bat species, providing essential foraging and commuting resources to local bat populations and connectivity with the wider environment, which is also of high suitability to bats," the survey said.

It said "loss of or disturbance" to roosts in trees on the grounds, which provide shelter for bats, would result in "adverse effects" on the local populations of two common and widespread species.

In Britain, all bat species and their roosts are legally protected, by law , meaning it is an offence to kill, injure, take or disturb a bat, or to destroy, damage, obstruct or otherwise interfere with a bat roost, breeding site or resting place.

NRW said it has not received an application for a protected species development licence at this stage, but Hammond confirmed plans to go through the process.

articles.title: Masked men block traffic to UK’s Port of Dover in apparent anti-immigrant protest
articles.summary: A group of masked men blocked roads leading to Britain’s busiest ferry port on Saturday in what officials said appeared to be an anti-immigration protest.
articles.body: A group of masked men blocked roads leading to Britain’s busiest ferry port on Saturday in what officials said appeared to be an anti-immigration protest. The Port of Dover said all traffic in and out was “stopped due to an ongoing public order incident,” and police said they were “engaging with the protesters.” Video posted on social media showed several dozen men in black, their faces covered, standing across a major road near the port. One clip showed demonstrators linking arms across a main road and shouting “stop the boats.” Chris Vinson, a Conservative Party local councilor, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related.” “I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating,” he said. The National Highways agency said the protest blocked routes to the port and caused a 4-mile (6.4-kilometer) traffic jam on Saturday morning. The Port of Dover said one road to the port had reopened by late morning. P&O Ferries, which runs services between Dover and Calais in France, said passengers who missed their ferry would be offered the next available crossing. Dover, about 70 miles (110 kilometers) southeast of London, dealt with more than 9 million passengers and 2 million freight vehicles in 2025, according to the port’s website. The town has been the site of previous anti-immigrant protests focused on migrants who cross the Channel from France in small boats. Some politicians, including Nigel Farage of hard-right party Reform UK, have seized on the issue. He branded the asylum seekers “an invasion” in a Friday speech. The Labour Party government says stepped-up law enforcement cooperation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing this year by more than 40% compared to 2025. Mike Tapp, a Labour lawmaker who represents Dover in Parliament, criticized “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.” “I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossing are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess,” he wrote on Facebook on Saturday. “Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”

articles.title: Israel must protect West Bank’s Palestinians amid settler pogroms: US envoy
articles.summary: Huckabee labels some of the settlers committing violence as ‘terrorists’ though analysts say his visit is ‘symbolic’.
articles.body:
United States ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has met with several local officials and residents in the occupied West Bank, including Palestinian Americans attacked in violent Israeli settler pogroms.

The diplomat said on Saturday that the Israeli government has a “responsibility” to ensure the safety of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank after a sharp rise in pogroms.

“One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that happens,” Huckabee told reporters on Saturday.

Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim , reporting from Turmus Aya in the occupied West Bank, said that Huckabee not only met local officials, “but also Palestinian Americans who live in the village of Turmus Aya and have been seeing firsthand the effects of settler pogroms and violence, part of the whole escalation by settlers in the occupied West Bank”.

“They want the US ambassador to relay the message that this is systematic violence being practised against Palestinians, that it’s continuing and that they need actual change,” Ibrahim said, noting that settlers in the area “wrote slogans not just against Palestinians, but also against him [Huckabee]”.

One person Huckabee met was US-Palestinian Ruwan Alqam, who relocated to Turmus Aya from the US state of Texas with her family four months ago.

But every time Alqam’s family leaves their occupied West Bank home, “we’re hit with roadblock after roadblock, settlers after settlers”, she told Al Jazeera, shortly after attending a morning meeting with Huckabee.

On a recent day trip to Nablus, the family was unable to return home as Israeli settlers attacked their car with rocks, Alqam said.

“They’re not being held accountable for their actions – endangering Palestinians is a fun activity for them,” Alqam said of the settlers, describing the violence committed as “not a minority” among Israelis.

Huckabee was “very receptive” to the experiences of Turmus Aya residents, Alqam said, adding: “We are in desperate need of attention here.”

Speaking to reporters afterwards, Huckabee said: “Our clear message is that crime is crime, terror is terror. When people do it, they should have an expectation that they will have severe consequences”.

Meanwhile, Alon Pinkas , a former Israeli ambassador, told Al Jazeera that Huckabee’s visit to the West Bank is “largely symbolic … because his visit, as much as it is covered by the media, is not going to change American policy”.

Huckabee has labelled some of the settlers committing violence as “terrorists”, which is a “clear message”, Pinkas said, particularly coming from an evangelical Christian who “believes in the Jewish rights over the West Bank”.

Nonetheless, the Trump administration “doesn’t seem to care enough” about settler pogroms or the rights of Palestinians for it to “actually pressure the Israeli government”, Pinkas said.

Settler pogroms in the West Bank have ⁠risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government, the most right wing in Israel’s history, took office in late 2022.

Settlements have also increased, despite being illegal under international law, with Israel advancing its plan for 627 settler units in the occupied West Bank , deepening its efforts to sever Palestinian ties to Jerusalem.

articles.body: Patrick Clancy broke his silence after a mistrial was declared in Lindsay Clancy’s case, saying the prospect of enduring another trial over the killings of their three children is "extraordinarily painful." "Patrick Clancy is grateful to the Court and to the jurors for their hard work, their commitment, and their perseverance. The loss of Patrick’s children is something from which he will never recover and from which there will never be closure," his attorney, David Meier, wrote in a statement issued on Patrick's behalf. "The prospect of reliving this tragedy through another trial is extraordinarily painful — for Patrick, for his family, and for all us," the statement concluded. Patrick Clancy has previously asked the public to forgive his ex-wife, who has admitted killing their three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. Her attorneys have argued she was legally insane due to postpartum psychosis. LINDSAY CLANCY'S EX-HUSBAND HAS QUIETLY REMARRIED AND STARTED OVER AMID HER MURDER TRIAL During the trial, Patrick Clancy testified about the day of the killings on Jan. 24, 2023. The children were killed while he was running errands that included picking up children's stool softener at a CVS store and takeout for dinner. They spoke on the phone while he was out. On Friday afternoon, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial in the high-profile murder case after jurors said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. It will now be up to prosecutors whether Clancy will be tried again. The jury spent a week deliberating at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, where supporters and onlookers gathered outside for days awaiting a possible verdict. articles.title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
articles.summary: Nigel Farage's admirers in the party are calling for a stronger operation as the party aims for power.
articles.body:
"We are still a bit of a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately.

It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now .

How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them?

"A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. But we need roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them too," this same senior figure adds.

The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money.

Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk'

Reform donations row overshadows party's moment to lay out big ideas

Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges

Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.

But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.

In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.

Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.

Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.

Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.

Reform wants to project itself as a prospective party of government.

And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.

Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.

But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes that "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."

There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.

Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.

Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.

Both James Orr, the party's head of policy; and Dan Jukes, Farage's right-hand man, will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.

Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.

Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.

Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.

Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.

The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

articles.title: Middlesbrough family pass down unopened selection box in memory of girl
articles.summary: A Middlesbrough dad has kept a selection box unopened for 36 years in memory of his daughter.
articles.body:
A selection box from the 1990s will remain uneaten in tribute to a young girl who died before she could receive it as a Christmas gift 36 years ago.

Susan Peacock, from Middlesbrough, was seven when she died in a car accident and her dad Stephen kept the Cadbury's chocolates she never opened in memory of her.

He has now passed the box on to Susan's twin sister Rachel who said she will preserve it "for as long as possible".

Rachel, 42, posted the vintage box of chocolates on social media and said she was overwhelmed by the "unbelievable" response from people with memories of loved ones who had bought them a similar gift for Christmas.

She said none of the chocolates had been eaten but one of the packets has slightly opened and "it doesn't smell too good".

"I will not be giving it a taste, I'm going to keep it for as long as possible," she said.

The chocolates have a best before date of June or July 1991 but they are in good condition after being stored in a cupboard and a bedroom drawer.

Stephen said he "couldn't chuck away anything of Susan's" but wanted to pass the chocolates on as he is getting older.

"It's a selection box but it is a memory, I kept everything of Susan's," he said.

"The selection box was bought years ago and I have always kept it, it was in the cupboard then I put it in the bed drawer."

Rachel said she "absolutely loves" the selection box because it is "a bit of Susan".

"I just don't want her to be forgotten," she said.

articles.title: US only country to oppose UN resolution correcting Africa’s size on world maps
articles.summary: The U.S. was the only country to not support a United Nations resolution adjusting the appearance of Africa and other regions on world maps. The body passed the “Correct the Map” initiative by a margin of 164 to one, with six nations abstaining from the vote. The resolution, which was introduced by the West African…
articles.body:
The U.S. was the only country to not support a United Nations resolution adjusting the appearance of Africa and other regions on world maps.

The body passed the “Correct the Map” initiative by a margin of 164 to one, with six nations abstaining from the vote.

The resolution , which was introduced by the West African country Togo, does not require the abandonment of the long-used Mercator projection. It instead encourages the use of equal-area projections that more accurately depict relative country sizes.

Yaryna Ferencevych, the deputy U.S. representative to the U.N. Economic and Social Council, said in a statement explaining the U.S.’s vote that this measure, “mocks the work and purpose of this institution.”

“Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th century, and their role in promoting reparations and ‘cognitive justice,’” she said.

“Resolutions like this and the ideological agenda they promote, are barnacles on our work here, and the reason this institution is losing its credibility,” Ferencevych continued. “When the United Nations questions why it is losing legitimacy in the world, and is not taken seriously, time and again, we point to resolutions such as this.”

The “Correct the Map” campaign has encouraged nations around the world to adopt the Equal Earth projection, which was designed by cartographers in 2018 to present a more proportionally accurate depiction of the world.

The African Union Commission said the initiative “marks a historic step toward accurate and equitable global cartographic representation.”

“For centuries, the Mercator projection distorted global geography, shrinking Africa to the size of Greenland when our continent is actually 14 times larger,” the group wrote on social media .

“Today’s resolution promotes equal-area maps like Equal Earth across classrooms, media, and international institutions ensuring the world map finally reflects Africa’s true scale, weight, and place in the world.”

articles.title: UK gov’t condemns masked anti-immigrant protesters blocking Dover port
articles.summary: Traffic at Britain’s largest international port briefly halted as ‘stop the boats’ protesters blocked approaching roads.
articles.body:
Dozens of masked people protesting Channel migrant crossings have blocked access to the port of Dover, briefly halting ferry traffic between England and France.

Images shared online showed dozens of demonstrators dressed in black and wearing balaclavas streaming onto roads surrounding the port in the United Kingdom on Saturday.

In an online livestream that appeared to be shot by one of the protesters, a crowd of black-clothed men chanted “stop the boats” as they faced a line of police.

The UK government condemned the action, saying it went beyond peaceful protest.

On Saturday morning, the Port of Dover said all traffic in and out was “stopped due to an ongoing public order incident”. At around noon, port managers said traffic was “free flowing” once again. P&O Ferries also confirmed that access to the port had been restored.

Local police said they were “engaging” with protesters, who had initially blocked “all routes” in and out of the terminal, used by ferries connecting southern England to northern France.

The National Highways agency said the protest blocked roads to the port and caused a 6.4km traffic jam on Saturday morning.

Local Conservative Party councillor, Chris Vinson, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”.

“I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating,” he said.

The Labour government said “the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused”.

“We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today,” the government statement said.

Britain is grappling with how to curb the perilous and politically contentious small-boat crossings, which in recent years have seen tens of thousands of migrants arriving annually on the shores of southeast England.

The issue has been relentlessly seized upon by the hard-right Reform UK party, which surged in popularity on the back of growing anti-immigration sentiment.

The centre-left Labour government has said that the number of boats carrying migrants and asylum seekers across the Channel was the lowest this summer since 2019, in part because of cooperation deals with the French government.

Dover is Britain’s largest international ferry port. During summer months there, it handles more than 10,000 freight vehicles and 15,000 passenger vehicles a day, accounting for a third of Britain’s goods trade with the European Union.

About 110km southeast of London, Dover handled more than nine million passengers and two million freight vehicles last year, according to the port’s website.

articles.title: Three Iranian tankers struck in retaliation for missile attacks, US military says
articles.summary: The United States military said Saturday its forces had struck three Iranian crude oil carriers after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles toward two US Navy warships.
articles.body: The United States military said Saturday its forces struck three Iranian crude oil carriers after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles toward two US Navy warships. The fresh exchanges threaten to heighten a shipping war in and beyond the Persian Gulf, as Iran seeks to prevent shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz without its consent and the US steps up targeting of Iranian shipping. The two sides traded strikes earlier this week for the first time in over a month and the new attacks risk another retaliatory cycle. “A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks,” the statement from US Central Command said on Saturday. In response, US forces “permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask.” Outside the Persian Gulf, according to CENTCOM, an unladen crude tanker called the M/T Kylo was “completely destroyed” after being hit multiple times to render it inoperable. “Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander. Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported the statement by US Central Command, adding that “Iranian officials emphasized that they would respond strongly to any attack.” But there has been no word from the Iranian leadership. Earlier Saturday, Iranian news agencies had said that a tanker came under missile attack by US forces near Kharg Island. The tanker was hit by four projectiles fired by US forces, Tasnim reported. There were no casualties, the agency added. Audio confirmed by CNN showed that a US military aircraft issued warnings to the ship via an emergency channel. In one, an American-accented voice says: “Motor Tanker STARK 1, this is the United States military aircraft. I am preparing to fire at your stern. You have 10 minutes to clear the crew from the stern of your ship. Over.” In a later exchange, the ship is warned: “This was your final warning… get into your lifeboats and abandon the ship immediately.” The conflict between Iran and the United States is in a volatile limbo, with both battling for control over the vital Strait of Hormuz, which is critical for global oil supplies. Kharg Island, a coral outcrop off Iran’s coast, has typically handled roughly 90% of the country’s crude oil exports. The island has been attacked throughout the conflict and US President Donald Trump has previously threatened to capture it. Shipping data and satellite imagery indicates there are nearly 20 Iranian tankers at anchor near Kharg, unable to exit the Gulf because of the US naval blockade but in many cases fully laden. In the Gulf as a whole and just beyond - in the Gulf of Oman - there are more than 50 Iranian tankers, according to ship tracking services. On Thursday, US Vice President JD Vance denied the conflict should even be described as a “war,” adding that despite the recent flare-up there was “no active shooting.” He also refused to lay out a timetable for ending the conflict, suggesting instead it was up to Iran to conclude the conflict that began with joint US-Israeli airstrikes six months ago.

articles.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
articles.summary: The Reform leader also told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg that his family are "begging" him to leave his job.
articles.body:
Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.

His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.

Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.

In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.

In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News , Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.

Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.

The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.

When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."

"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.

"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."

The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.

Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.

Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.

But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.

"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.

He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".

Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.

Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.

He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."

Analysis: Farage may have to pay more attention

There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

articles.title: US says it hit Iran oil tankers helping finance ‘regional proxies’
articles.summary: US strikes have hit Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg island.
articles.body:
The United States military says it has struck three Iranian oil tankers after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships in regional waters.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded multiple Iranian attacks on Saturday.

CENTCOM said its attack on Iranian oil carriers came after the IRGC fired ballistic missiles towards the two US warships “patrolling regional waters”. It said no personnel had been injured.

The US strikes hit Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg island. The US military said it disabled two Iranian crude oil carriers and destroyed a third, targeting vessels it claims were part of a multibillion-dollar network that finances the IRGC and its “regional proxies”.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

CENTCOM did not immediately provide further details about whether the strikes on the tankers caused casualties.

The strikes come a day after US President Donald Trump said the conflict, which has resulted in the deaths of 18 US service members and a spike in global energy prices, is “small potatoes” .

Both sides have tried to inflict economic and military pain on the other, with negotiations having collapsed to end the six-month war that the US and Israel began. Almost a week ago, the US and Iran exchanged attacks after a month without direct confrontations.
